en: The Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty spoke these words, which were recorded by his disciple Guanding.
Next, to clarify the gains and losses regarding internal heterodoxy: the Three Baskets and Four Gates are fundamentally intended for entering into principle.

If one clings to these as established doctrines, they become mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). Although he developed insight and attained meditative concentration while also mastering the scriptures,
if he had merely held fast to this gateway as his own position, it would have resulted only in the production of wholesome roots.
Once associated with views, they further give rise to the three types of conduct.
Those whose conduct is wholesome exclusively create karmic retribution for the sake of various states of existence;
by grasping at the gateway of existence, they give rise to craving and aversion.
The victor falls into the pit of pride; the vanquished falls into the prison of sorrow.
Born into a place of affliction, the door of existence is closed once more, and liberation cannot be attained.
Those who practice evil deeds hold that what they do is right and everything else is wrong; for this reason,
there is no evil they will not commit through the gate of existence.
When malevolent spirits enter the mind, they only increase various transgressions;
among the ninety-six paths, only three accord with the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, there are the path of the Abhidharma and the path of the Sūtras.
Yet five hundred arhats were able to emerge through this gate of existence;
how could it possibly be something perverse?
Nowadays, people take a biased view and believe that ghosts enter the mind.
Therefore, they are called *abhidharma* ghosts.
They may enter through [wrong] views or enter through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
For those who practice it themselves, there is one; for those who manifest emanations (*nirmāṇa*), there are also four.
As it is with one gate, so it is with the other three;
whether through the Shared, Distinct, or Perfect [teachings], each possesses four gates that give rise to views,
and each view likewise comprises the three practices.
Those who practice good may be known;
as for those who practice evil,
they maintain within the Mahāyāna that sensual desire itself is the path.
Within the three poisons are contained all the Buddha-dharmas.
While such true words fundamentally extinguish afflictions,
if one takes them up with partiality and attachment, the fetters and karma will arise once more.
They engage in praise and blame, sorrow and attachment, deceit and arrogance, and growling rivalry for fame and profit.
Their own practice consists of one [type of] transformation, while their influence on others consists of four;
since these are neither untainted nor moistened by ignorance, they constitute karma.
Driven by the power of karma, there is nowhere one will not be reborn;
the details cannot be fully recounted, but it may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Such views as these run counter to the Noble Path.
Furthermore, it can give rise to various transgressions.
Those who do not recognize this cling to it, claiming it is the Path;
even if they know it is such a view, they follow that view and thereby bury themselves.
How could one cultivate the factors of enlightenment by viewing [the mind] as either moving or unmoving?
Briefly stated, such views give rise to various faults.
Second, the clarification and resolution of the true and the false.
First, a definitive resolution regarding the phenomena that arise;
second, a definitive resolution regarding the phenomena upon which they depend.
Now, this is universally applied to the four propositions of the external non-Buddhist paths.
Even up to the four gates of the perfected non-Buddhist views that penetrate the Vedas, and even up to the three foundations of mindfulness and the three doors of liberation of the perfected gate—
their names and numbers are identical,
yet there is no difference in the faults and fetters arising from the views they give rise to.
It is like two chains, one of gold and one of iron;
furthermore, it ranges from the four propositions of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) up to the four views of the Perfect Gate (vṛttamukha).
Although their names are pure and beautiful,
the essence of the afflictions they give rise to is defiled;
it is like the two raw blocks of jade and mouse-dung.
Furthermore, from the four propositions of the non-Buddhists up to the four views of the Perfect Gate, although both involve refinement and cultivation, there is success and failure;
it is like the milk of a cow and a donkey.
Furthermore, from the four views of the non-Buddhists up to the four views of the Perfect Gate regarding harm and non-harm,
they are like the two fruits, the kāra and the tinduka.
The self (ātman) as it is conceptualized is merely a phenomenon of bondage and is not a sovereign self.
Each person clings to their own view as true and regards others' views as false;
thus, they engage in mutual disputes of right and wrong—what relevance does this have to reality as it truly is?
Claiming for oneself that the true path has been opened, yet one still falls back into the cycle of existence;
hoping to attain nirvana, one instead sinks deeper into birth and death.
Proclaiming one's words to be correct and true, one ultimately ends up in heterodoxy and deviation.
Affection arises toward objects of affection;
aversion arises toward objects of aversion.
Although one may give rise to compassion and love, it is merely the perception of compassion and pity.
Although one may find peace, it is through the severing of afflictions that birth and death are overcome;
though one may possess all-knowledge, it is through the worldly estimation of circumstances;
and although one may attain supernormal powers, they consist of both fundamental transformations and tainted transformations.
The Vedas one studies and the doctrines taught by worldly sages are not the power of dhāraṇī, nor are they the flow of the Dharma-realm;
though they may sever the dull afflictions, they are like the inchworm.
The treatments administered by worldly physicians may bring temporary relief, yet the illness recurs;
the ocean of the eighty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*) is vast and boundless,
and the wheel of birth and death within the three realms has no limit.
To remain submerged in outflows with no prospect of ever emerging is entirely due to the illusory falsehoods of various views;
how could these possibly constitute the path of ultimate reality?
Second, regarding the difference based on the dharmas upon which they rely:
all views each rely on their respective dharmas.
Third, external non-Buddhists are persons with outflows (*sāsrava*).
When one gives rise to tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) with a tainted mind, one becomes attached to those objects of attachment.
Both the object of attachment and the mind that attaches are, in their very essence, contentious strife;
it is not merely a matter of seizing someone by the head and pulling out their hair at the time of an argument.
Having given rise to various views, they claim these to be *nirvāṇa*.
Clinging to these established views increases the fierce poison of contention and strife;
the dharmas upon which they rely are not true, and the views they have produced are likewise false.
Although this is a heterodox teaching, if one skillfully grasps its underlying intent and enters the correct state through its heterodox forms—
just as a flower may fly or a leaf may move by virtue of slight causes and conditions, yet still lead one to realize the stage of a Pratyekabuddha—
how much more so would this apply to the established dharmas of the world?
However, although the Pratyekabuddhas correctly utilize the flowers and leaves, they are ultimately not the True Teaching.
While the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) may have secretly attained some realization,
their dharma-gates merely lead to various views.
This is not the True Dharma.
It all arises from attachment—the mind clinging to dharmas of attachment—wherein cause and effect both contend.
This establishes the nature of false dharma and gives rise to false views.
If the Three Piṭakas and Four Gates are the supramundane dharmas attained by supramundane sages,
and their essence is purity— the locus for extinguishing afflictions—
then it is not only the Buddhist sūtras that constitute the True Dharma.
Five hundred practitioners were also able to attain the Way.
The *Miaoshengding lun* (Treatise on the Sublime Samādhi) states that one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [this occurred].
One hundred thousand people left the household life, and ninety thousand attained the Way.
In the second century, one hundred thousand people left the household life,
and ten thousand attained the Way.
One should know that with a mind free from attachment, one does not cling even to the dharma of non-attachment.
One should resolve to awaken to the true nature of impermanence:
that every thought-moment arises and ceases, such that one cannot preserve the morning until the evening.
One who aspires to seek the essential point does not block the gates, lest they give rise to conceptual proliferation through defilement.
It is like a person who wishes to see the king quickly,
receive his bounty, and be invested with office, yet enters through all four gates.
What leisure is there to linger over debating whether things are superior or inferior?
Knowing that the gate is a common path, there is no need for such debate.
It is like medicine used to treat illness; one should not engage in discrimination.
Swiftly emerge from the burning house to reach the end of all suffering.
When true illumination arises, one realizes the ultimate path, which is ultimately free from contention.
Where there is no contention, there is no karma; where there is no karma, there is no birth and death.
When there is only the Way, the mind-ground is extinguished and becomes level and expansive;
cause and effect both cease to exist, and strife is entirely extinguished.
There is only right view and no false view.
Furthermore, although these four gates are the True Dharma,
if one approaches them with an attached mind,
one will give rise to false views.
Seeing the differences at the four gates,
they frequently engage in strife and contention during the time of cultivating the causes;
it is like someone who has lived for a long time by a city gate.
One discriminates between tiles and wood, evaluating them as superior or inferior, refined or coarse—
saying the south is right while the north is wrong, or that the east is skillful while the west is clumsy.
To cause oneself to linger and refuse to move forward is not the fault of the gate.
The author is likewise so:
he discriminates names and characteristics, has extensive knowledge of afflictions, and recites many sections of the Path;
yet he merely collects essential terms and uses them as a medium for self-promotion in his quest for renown.
Beating the great drum of self-importance and erecting the banner of pride,
they boast to one another and engage in mutual strife,
seizing each other by the head and plucking out their hair.
The eighty-eight afflictions (*anuśaya*) of hatred and craving are vast and pervasive;
they all arise from clinging to the mind within the gateway of the True Dharma, thereby giving birth to false views.
The defilements thus produced are no different from those of the external non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The dharmas reckoned by the treatises differ as vastly as heaven and earth.
As the Vaipulya sūtras state:
"Various questions posed by those who act as bridges are censured by the Wise."
Human beings are also like this.
For the sake of studying the Way, they practice these four gates;
yet after more than thirty years, they have not yet clearly understood even a single gate through their analysis.
The moment one applies effort, the years have already grown old.
Without the three flavors, one lives in vain and dies in vain, casting away this single lifetime in emptiness.
It is like that question regarding the bridge: what benefit is there?
This arises from giving rise to false views by clinging to the mind and to the dharmas of non-clinging.
Next, the essence of the four gates of the Shared Teaching (Pāryāyika-yāna) is the True Dharma;
it is proximate to the transformation city and precedes this direct path.
Although skillfulness and clumsiness differ, there is no distinction in the point of passage.
It is like a celestial gate that is straight and magnificent, while other gates are curved and humble;
one does not dwell in either gate, yet gains access and proceeds through both.
If both counting and the two— tiles and wood—
are equally free from delay and congestion, and if one is without contention or attachment regarding the dharma-gate, whether cause or effect,
this is called the unattached mind.
One who does not cling to the dharma of non-clinging will not give rise to false views.
Furthermore, if one clings to this direct gate with a mind of attachment, one also gives rise to false views;
or one may differentiate the characteristics of the gate for the sake of fame, for the sake of the assembly, for the sake of superiority, or for the sake of profit.
The fetters of hatred, craving, and pride arise because of this;
it is like putting poison into good medicine—
how could one not die?
Because those attached to views allow poison to enter the True Dharma, they increase the accumulation of suffering; this is not the fault of the Tathāgata.
Those of sharp faculties among the non-Buddhists may enter the correct characteristics by means of false characteristics.
They cause those who are unattached to become attached, turning them into disciples of the Buddha;
they cause those of dull faculties within the inner path to enter the heterodox through correct signs,
making the unattached attached and turning them into heterodox disciples.
How tragic it is! Whether through the four gates of the Distinct or Perfect teachings—be they skillful or clumsy, sharp or dull—all lead to ultimate nirvana.
Because one does not dwell in attachment to the cause, there is no contention in the fruit.
If one gives rise to views by sealing off [the truth], then afflictions will arise, as they did for Uluṅka and others.
Observing it from this perspective, one is like a person with clear vision standing at the confluence of the Jing and Wei rivers;
how could one allow oneself to be confused by names and fail to recognize what is clear and what is turbid?
Briefly clarifying the arousal of vision, there are five sections;
each section contains four parts,
resulting in twenty gates.
There are seven [categories] within each gate,
totaling one hundred and forty different views;
these are discussed extensively in immeasurable detail.
All are developed by relying upon causes and conditions.
This is because, by universally practicing *śamatha*, all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are developed;
and by universally practicing *vipaśyanā*, all insights (*darśana*) are developed.
The conditions for universal cultivation arise from *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*,
whereas the fundamental, specific causes must stem from previous lives—
perhaps having studied among the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
Some are disciples of the Buddha who have studied within the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna;
some have given rise to various views due to hearing the characteristics of dharmas;
and some have given rise to these various views while practicing seated meditation.
Due to being forgotten across successive lifetimes, understanding does not manifest; yet now,
by cultivating a tranquil mind or hearing the sūtras and śāstras, one’s past karma is perfumed, and upon seeing the Dharma, realization arises once again.
That which was matured in previous lives now manifests easily;
that which was unripe in previous lives now manifests with difficulty.
That which is distant across many lifetimes is difficult to manifest, whereas that which is near is easy.
If external objects are mature and near, they appear first;
if internal objects are mature and near, they manifest first.
Since supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and the Vedas are both phenomena of objective characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).
That which is separated by a lifetime is easily forgotten and difficult to manifest;
that which is seen is of the nature of wisdom, difficult to forget and easy to manifest.
It is like a person who, after a long separation, remembers the name but forgets the face.
The difficulty or ease of the matter and principle is likewise so.
If there were external conditions involving ghosts in a previous life,
then ghosts will afflict one, causing the arousal of ghost-dhyāna and the manifestation of ghost-vision.
Externally there are auspicious conditions;
the Sage bestows upon them the arising of right insight through meditation.
Furthermore, if one has not previously recognized the faults and afflictions of various views, [one cannot attain this].
When fear arises toward what is seen, one hastily and urgently cuts it off;
now that you recognize its false nature, be careful not to cut it off abruptly.
Rather, allow it to develop freely so that it may serve as a power to assist the Path; there will surely be great benefit.
It is like having a parasite in the stomach: one must first nourish the "inch-long white worm" before expelling the "trunk-bead.
The reason for this is that the ignorant people of the world are as stubborn as oxen and horses.
In vain they thunder with the sound of the Dharma and spread forth embroidered rhetoric;
these bring no benefit to their hearing or vision.
They are addicted to the five desires like those afflicted by a chronic parasite-disease.
If one gives rise to various views, these dull underlying tendencies (anuśaya) may be compared to a speck of white on a fingernail;
yet when the wisdom of insight is adjacent to right contemplation, the Dharma is easily realized upon hearing it,
like that pearl in the hot water.
For this reason, one must cultivate views and refine the mind to act as a vanguard and guide.
If one enters the Two Vehicles, one moves views while cultivating the factors of enlightenment;
if one enters the Mahāyāna, one does not move views while cultivating the factors of enlightenment.
Only after defeating the invaders and crushing the rebels is one's merit completed;
this constitutes nurturing external views to serve as attendants.
If one gives rise to the views of the Three Pitakas or the clumsy views of the Four Gates, [the same applies].
One penetrates through the skillful vision of the four gates.
Although this vision is an obstruction, it is also profoundly supportive of the path.
If one’s merit leads to rebirth in heaven, it is very easy [to attain], yet attaining the Path remains difficult.
Seeing this nature of wisdom,
even those submerged in samsara can easily awaken to the Way with great rapidity.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The three evil destinies are also not mentioned because those who attain the Way there are few;
furthermore, one with white skin and black moles is not called a "black person.
Once it is known that these are delusions of view, one must not allow arbitrary discrimination to arise.

Just as those non-Buddhists who previously possessed views were enlightened the moment they saw the shadow of the whip when converted by the Buddha— like a swift horse that perceives the whip’s shadow—
if one lacks such views, ten thousand axes cannot sever them.
It is like preaching the Dharma to oxen and horses;
they do not understand it. If even the barbarians and outcasts do not yet understand the language, how could one discuss the profound mysteries with them?
Therefore, for such persons, the Buddha does not appear in the world;
rather, he manifests various forms and emanates his essence to act as their teacher and friend, guiding them to perceive the Dharma.
This is like the sun of the Buddha first rising.
As for "expedient means" (*upāya*), it refers to those who hear the Dharma and attain awakening immediately upon hearing it.
When the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of "secretly dispatching two persons," this refers,
in terms of the Dharma, to the two teachings of expedient means.
Regarding ordinary people, the provisional [teaching] is the same as that for the two vehicles;
even the various sages, through their skillful means, still instruct them in this view.
Now that they have attained the arising of vision, how could it be appropriate to suddenly eliminate it?
If, in previous lives, one cultivated the eight gates of the Separate and Complete Teachings but had not yet severed the pervasive delusions,
then when this view arises, its faults are the same as those of the three external paths.
If, however, in previous lives one has already destroyed the pervasive delusions...
If one has not yet realized the distinct principle, one may be equal to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*);
if even their prior views are still being nurtured, how much more so this view?
Vimalakīrti took the extreme faults of the two vehicles and refuted them as belonging to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Furthermore, recruit those who assist in the peripheral matters to serve as attendants;
interpret their advances and retreats with flexibility rather than with one-sidedness.
Now, in this life, for those who cultivate the Way and give rise to the awakened mind, the ultimate truth may be expected.
If one has not yet given rise to [insight], the holy realm is difficult to realize.
Fourth, regarding the application of insight and cultivation to cessation and contemplation:
as discussed above in the general discourse, there are differences in how one attains insight.
Thus, there are one hundred and forty types.
If categorized separately according to internal heterodoxy, there are one hundred and twelve types.
As for the schools established to clarify their tenets, how many schools are there in total?
Within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the conceptual views and characteristics of systems such as Sāṃkhya are subsumed;
are they identical or different?
To what extent do their paths of deviation and correctness differ in quality and degree?
If one understands this intent, one knows that they are not mutually exclusive;
for those who do not understand it, what else can they know?
Generally, the Buddha’s Dharma employs two modes of exposition: first, inclusive synthesis, and second, analytical deconstruction.
As in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*, not praising or disparaging [others] is the meaning of "gathering" (*saṃgraha*).
In the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, wielding weapons and even decapitating others is the meaning of "breaking" (*bhañjana*).
Although giving and taking follow different paths, both serve to bring about benefit.
If those who flow along with various views must have them severed and brought to an end;
if those who assist in refining the spirit and turning the mind toward the correct path can all be accepted—
these aforementioned views are explained in reference to these various types of persons.
There is not a single person who manifests them all simultaneously.
Even if they were all to manifest, they would merely devour one another; there is only this single reality.
According to each individual manifestation, each constitutes a dharma-gate.
Through skillful means, he demonstrated various verbal methods over a period of ninety days;
yet, when gathered together, each vision is identical to the single gate of contemplation.
It encompasses all phenomena without end, and its manifold sovereignty is singular.
Now, let us briefly consider one view; many others are likewise.
Among all views, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) alone can destroy them all, yet nothing can destroy emptiness. This leads people toward a profound benefit.
Now, one should first contemplate the analogy of the views of emptiness through ten points.
Regarding the realm of contemplation:
the views of emptiness give rise to the dharmas of the ten dharma-realms.
A bitter melon is not heat that can act as a cause of disease;
emptiness is not the ten realms that can act as causes and conditions.
The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* says:
The Abhidharma clarifies that the arising of a mind of wrong view in a single kṣaṇa is itself unwholesome.
In a single kṣaṇa, the mind arises as wrong view.
That which is neither wholesome nor unwholesome is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
All wholesome and unwholesome states arise based on the motivating mind (samutthāpaka-citta) as their cause.
Now, this view of emptiness also has two meanings.
If one contemplates it separately,
it arises from the causes of the ten dharma-realms, such as their conditions of origination.
Why is this? Previously, when one had not yet seen emptiness, one never practiced these [three] activities;
now that one has given rise to the view of emptiness, there are immediately three activities.
As previously stated,
those who commit evil by means of emptiness practice the dharma of non-obstruction;
they do not perceive above them any sūtras or the field of merit of the Buddha as worthy of veneration.
Those of the lower grade fail to perceive the virtue of parental kindness;
they practice the ways of naked beasts and sever all mundane and supramundane goodness.
Although icchantikas are evil, they still retain a trace of the goodness of compassionate affection.
The view of emptiness is eternally devoid of the three grades of purely evil karma.
Rebellious harm, injury, and destruction constitute the realm of hell;
lack of shame and lack of remorse constitute the realm of animals.
Those who are stingy and greedy, who violate the precepts of the fast, and who maintain themselves through impure means, belong to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Because they violate the fast, they are perpetually hungry;
because they are impure, they consume filth.
Regarding those who practice virtue based on emptiness:
when they adorn the ten wholesome paths of action with the precepts and ascetic practices, their three karmas become fully matured, which constitutes the realm of the three wholesome destinies;
furthermore, when they give rise to the fundamental [wholesome roots], this constitutes the realm of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, regarding those who become śrāvakas by means of emptiness:
if one says they are empty, it is because they do not actually understand the Four Noble Truths within emptiness. Why is this so?
If one realizes that the nature of phenomena is empty and pure,
then false views regarding emptiness must necessarily depend upon karmic retribution;
such retribution consists of defiled form.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Whether form is permanent or impermanent, and so forth, all such [attributes] depend upon form;
the emptiness that receives and contains it is distinct from these others."
Apprehending the empty image as distinct from existent phenomena, one gives rise to three types of conceptualization directed toward emptiness; this mind of emptiness is superior to other phenomena.
This is called the five aggregates.
The sense-object of space confronting the mind constitutes two bases (āyatana);
when the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is further added,
these constitute the three realms (dhātu).
The elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and aggregates (skandha) are themselves the truth of suffering.
The view of emptiness is the locus of hatred, the locus of craving, and the locus of pride;
whereas the weak view of existence merely tears apart the phenomena of existence.
If one grasps the principle and reaches emptiness, doubt cannot arise.
If one cannot tear it apart by seizing it and it does not come forth through such grasping, then one will growl with suspicion.
Furthermore, although there may be no doubt now, there shall be great doubt later.
Why is this? If emptiness were the ultimate principle, it should be equal to the noble ones;
since it is not equal, how can one not harbor doubt?
Who is it that conceives of emptiness? It is the "self" that conceives of emptiness.
Yet, in reality, the self is not empty, nor is emptiness the self.
It is because of emptiness that the self arises.
That is to say, one thinks, "I act," "I understand," "I am praised," or "I am reviled.
Clinging to this extreme of emptiness, one cannot relinquish it;
that is, one hopes to attain nirvana by means of the path of emptiness.
Thus, taking emptiness as one's precept is not [the same as] regarding non-causes such as the "chicken-and-dog" practices as causes;
this is the grasping of precepts and observances based on theft of the true cause.
To reckon emptiness as emptiness is not logically correct; to reckon that which is not the fruit as the fruit is the view of grasping at what is not the fruit as the fruit.
A biased view of emptiness is precisely wrong view.
Thus, these ten proclivities arise from emptiness. In the lower realm of the desire realm, there are ten [proclivities] in the section on suffering;
in the section on origin, there are seven, excluding the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, and the attachment to precepts and rituals.

Below the Path (mārga), there are eight [factors] excluding the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa). Below Cessation (nirodha), there are seven, excluding the view of a self-identity and the clinging to precepts and observances.
Together, these total thirty-two.
In the realms of form and formlessness, four instances of hatred are excluded from each,
resulting in twenty-eight for each;
together, there are eighty-eight *anuśaya*s (proclivities).
This is called the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Delusion accumulates and suffering arises; suffering is produced by origination.
Long-nailed (Dīrghanakha) did not recognize this flow and circulation of the accumulation of suffering.
Furthermore, there is another ghost whose head is ablaze with fire.
Even those from the realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception have not yet escaped this;
how could one remain in emptiness while failing to recognize suffering and its origin?
If one perceives emptiness through consciousness, then both suffering and its origin depend upon form (*rūpa*).
All phenomena of form are called the body;
the body and form are defiled, and this defilement is impurity.
That which the wise loathe— the destruction of the inversion regarding purity—

is called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). If one holds the view of emptiness regarding sensation (*vedanā*), this is "sensation that is not the sensation of sensation," which is the second phrase.
Conformity with emptiness is pleasant feeling;
opposition to emptiness is painful feeling;
that which is neither opposed nor conforming is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The three feelings are themselves the three sufferings.
To reckon suffering as pleasure is called a perversion.
If one knows that there is no pleasure and thereby destroys the perversion of pleasure, this is called the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
When emptiness and sensory objects encounter the mind, mental consciousness arises.
This mind undergoes arising and ceasing, flowing and surging anew at every moment.
When there is an object-condition, thought arises; when there is no object-condition, thought does not arise.
To claim that what is subject to arising and ceasing and is impermanent is permanent is an inversion.
To cognize that consciousness is impermanent and thereby destroy the inversion of permanence is called the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
One grasps at the empty appearance of formations and, amidst the performance of wholesome and unwholesome deeds,
conceives of a self. If these formations were the self, then when the formations have good and bad qualities,
or when they arise and cease, the self would likewise be subject to such states.
If the self were all-pervasive throughout the infinite conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), then the self would be infinite.
If it were not all-pervasive, then there would be no self in a single phenomenon,
nor would there be a self in the multitude of phenomena.
To falsely reckon that there is a self is precisely a perversion (*viparyāsa*).
If one knows there is no self, then the conceptualization [of a self] is destroyed; this is called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
However, all the aggregates (*skandha*) collectively involve the four perversions.
One strongly conceives of a self in relation to perception and formations;
one strongly conceives of purity in relation to form;
and one strongly conceives of permanence in relation to the mind.
When one calculates pleasure with respect to feeling,
it is called the specific application of mindfulness;
this is not the case for the general application of mindfulness.
This is the application of mindfulness through the arising of the view of emptiness;
diligent effort to break through perverted views is precisely the right exertion;
and cultivating this within a concentrated mind is called the bases of psychic power.
The arising of the five roots of goodness is called "roots" (mūla).

The application of the path of peace is called the "seven factors of enlightenment" (saptabodhyaṅga).
Practicing within the path of peace and security is called the Eightfold Noble Path.
This constitutes the view of emptiness that can give rise to the Truth of the Path.

Once the view of emptiness is established, suffering and its origin are fully understood.
The view that suffering and its origin are not ultimately empty is destroyed by the mind that realizes emptiness;

Because the self cannot be found, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is destroyed.
Because the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is destroyed, the view of a self (ātmadṛṣṭi) is destroyed.
Because the view of a self is destroyed, the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) is destroyed.
The view of emptiness as a path and the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) are destroyed.

Because the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) are refuted, the eighty-eight proclivities are refuted.
Because the eighty-eight afflictions (*anuśaya*) are destroyed, the "bond of the seed" (*bīja-bandhana*) is destroyed.
Because the bond of the seed is destroyed, one is able to realize the first fruit and progress toward becoming an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*).
When the "bond of the fruit" (*phala-bandhana*) is destroyed, one enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
This is the arising and ceasing of the view of emptiness;

If one clearly understands the Four Noble Truths within the view of emptiness, then one knows the true path for the exhaustion of suffering.

This extends even to the one hundred and forty kinds of views,
whether taken individually or collectively, including the view that is beyond words.
They all recognize the true path and are able to move within and emerge from among various views.
Were it otherwise, they would not perceive the Four Noble Truths.
For this reason, one has long wandered through the great ocean of suffering of birth and death.
If one can perceive the Four Noble Truths, then one will attain the cessation of birth and death;
once existence has been exhausted, one shall no longer undergo further existences.
This is precisely what is meant by that.
Next, regarding the explanation of the Pratyekabuddha who gives rise to the view of emptiness:

Perversion is itself ignorance.

Because no new [karma] is produced, grasping and becoming do not arise;

As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

Grasping arises from craving; it is associated with craving, joy, aversion, pride, and doubt.

Craving arises because feeling gives rise to craving.

Just as one experiences the relish and pursuit of the flavor of a single dharma, one knows that feeling has contact as its cause; it is through the presence of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) and the encounter with objects that contact is obtained.
As the Sūtra says:
With contact as a condition, various sensations arise.

because the sense objects touch the sense faculties, the sense bases are established.
Entry occurs through the three factors of name-and-form and the kalala; as for form,

which life-force is able to maintain and sustain.
Consciousness has the name of the four aggregates;

Consciousness arises from past karma, and karma arises from ignorance.
Ignorance is the inversion of the past,
consisting of all views such as "existence" and "non-existence."
Thus, one is able to accomplish the physical body of this present life.
As the Sūtra says:
"Consciousness is the seed, karma is the field, and craving is the water."
Enveloped by ignorance, the sprout of name-and-form arises;
now, further deluded by the inverted view of emptiness, one performs wholesome and unwholesome deeds,

Perversion leads further to perversion;
ignorance leads further to ignorance;
they serve as causes and conditions for one another without end.

They exist due to the conjunction of the causes and conditions of false conceptualization.

Regarding "the views of emptiness, ignorance, old age, and death being quiescent":

Chan Master Bige attained the realization of the view of emptiness.
They mostly fall into the net and are unable to extricate themselves.

The ten fetters and so forth are the origin;
the foundations of mindfulness and so forth are the path;
the destruction of the four inversions is cessation.
Based on this, he made a vow:
"In the course of one day and one night,
how many hundreds of thousands of billions of aggregates (skandhas) are produced?"
Each and every of the five aggregates is itself a sentient being.
This is true for every day and night;
how much more so for an entire lifetime?
How much more so over immeasurable eons?
Since this is the case for the view of emptiness, it is likewise for all other views;
for the views capable of producing [afflictions] are already numerous.
The aggregates produced [by sentient beings] are incalculable;
if this is so for even a single person, how much more so for many.
This constitutes the vow: "I vow to deliver infinite sentient beings."
Just as the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) arise in every thought-moment for one who holds the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*),
so too do the other three views, such as the sixty-two [wrong] views, involve these eighty-eight proclivities.
If this is the case for even a single person, how much more so for many?
This is called the vow to sever the immeasurable afflictions.

this is the inexhaustible vow to know the Dharma-gate.

If the suffering and its accumulation of sentient beings were substantial in nature, they could not be delivered.
Because suffering and its accumulation arise from causes and conditions and lack intrinsic nature,
the ocean of suffering can be dried up and the source of accumulation can be easily exhausted.
Therefore, it is said that they "cross over.
As explained above, one contemplates emptiness and gives rise to vows;
regarding the practice arising from emptiness:
If one practices giving while clinging to the view of emptiness,
this is the "demon's gift.

If one who clings to the view of emptiness were to observe the precepts,

one is able to subdue both that view of emptiness and the sixty-two [wrong views].

it is a regression into the three miserable realms rather than progress.

By means of these supernormal powers, he exhorts and transforms sentient beings, causing them to abandon views and enter meditative concentration.

By extensively giving rise to the body of merit through vows and practices, one causes the flesh to grow while removing that fat, out of compassion for sentient beings.

This is called the arising of the six perfections within the dharma-realm from the view of emptiness.
To contemplate the view of emptiness is itself ignorance; ignorance is itself emptiness.
All the origins of suffering arising from ignorance are ultimately unfindable. Why is this?
The four perversions are merely false conceptualizations; how could they possess any inherent nature or reality?
Since the inversions to be remedied do not exist,
how can the foundations of mindfulness that remedy them be obtained?
Up to and including the factors of enlightenment, since they are all non-arising, they cannot be obtained.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"One should practice in accordance with suffering, emptiness, and so forth," and so on.
The followers of the Two Vehicles realize that these are empty, thereby severing suffering and entering extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
The Bodhisattva, being emptiness itself, yet possesses compassion, vows, and practice, vowing to deliver all sentient beings;
though they deliver sentient beings, it is as if delivering empty space;
though they extinguish afflictions, it is as if engaging in combat with the void.
Although dharmas arise, they arise like space;
although sentient beings cease, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa.
This wisdom, this abandonment—this is the bodhisattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
This is called the dharma-realm of the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching who give rise to the view of emptiness.
One contemplates that this view of emptiness possesses immeasurable characteristics;
that is to say, the analytical calculations regarding the Four Noble Truths are inexhaustible.
This inexhaustibility arises from the view of emptiness;
the view of emptiness arises from ignorance.
That which is produced is immeasurable, and that which produces it is likewise immeasurable.
Since that which produces is a provisional designation, that which is produced is likewise a provisional designation.
Inferring this ignorance to arise from the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is like recognizing that a dream arises because of sleep.
By contemplating this view of emptiness, one recognizes the true nature (dharmatā).
This true nature is the Tathāgatagarbha;
it is the principle of this treasury that is shrouded by immeasurable adventitious defilements.
Cultivating *dharma*-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to manifest the nature of purity is called the teaching for those with the view of emptiness who give rise to distinctions.

Furthermore, the afflictions of view are as vast as forty li of water,
while the residual force of the afflictions of thought is like a single drop of water.
All the aforementioned expedient means treat the afflictions of view together.
The exhaustion of delusions is called "entry into the stream," wherein one proceeds spontaneously without regression.
Since the delusions of view are difficult to eliminate, they require skillful means.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
Emptiness is used to remedy delusion.
If one can enter through the remedy of emptiness, there is no need to wait for other methods;
if one does not enter, what further remedy could be devised?
Just as fire arising within water cannot be extinguished by that very water,
how can emptiness treat the fault of the view of emptiness?
Now one knows that the view of emptiness is itself a disease of suffering and its origin.
Thereafter, one treats them with the wisdom of discernment:
the wisdom of impermanence according to the Tripiṭaka,
and the wisdom of emptiness according to the Shared Vehicle.
In all cases, first eliminate views;
specifically, one also first eliminates views to enter emptiness.
Next, through skillful means, one emerges from the *tathatā* (suchness), like planting a tree within emptiness.
Although Yuan does not intentionally eliminate the view of views, he eliminates it spontaneously;
he eliminates the tenacious views through various methods of treatment.
Why, then, do you say that emptiness alone is used as the remedy?
How do various remedies collectively treat a single view?
It is like using four kinds of medicine for a cold ailment:
by consuming ginger and cinnamon, the disease is removed and strength is restored.
Those who take the Five Stones eliminate illness and enhance their complexion;
those who take the Chonglou increase their lifespan and are able to fly;
those who take the Golden Elixir become Great Immortals.
When illnesses are of the same kind, the medicinal methods differ, and the resulting efficacy also differs.
The four teachings treat views differently, and the liberation through the exhaustion of views likewise differs.
Just as it is with the treatment of views, so it is with the treatment of other afflictions.
These four remedies are precisely the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
The *Śāsanopadeśa* (Teaching of the Bequeathed Instructions) commands that one rely on the four foundations of mindfulness to cultivate the path and emerge from the burning house. Why is this so?
The single view of emptiness is itself the triple world.
Within the triple world there are no separate dharmas; it is created solely by this one mind.
From the arising of the view of emptiness, one generates karma for the six realms, receives bodies in the six realms, and dwells in the abodes of the six realms.
The dwelling place is a burning house;
the body is a vessel of suffering;
karma is a malevolent spirit.
By vying with one another to push and pull the three carts, they drive them themselves and are thus able to escape.
These three carts are the three vehicles (*triyāna*) within the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*),
as well as the three types of persons within the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyayāna*).
The shared single foundation of mindfulness (*ekasmṛtyupasthāna*),
as well as the three types of foundations of mindfulness within the distinct skillful means,
are all truly one kind of foundation of mindfulness.
Furthermore, the single, perfect foundation of mindfulness briefly explains nine kinds of the four foundations of mindfulness,
while the middle [treatise] explains nine kinds of the factors of enlightenment.
The ninefold exposition of the Four Noble Truths shows that these foundations of mindfulness can all remedy views and enable one to escape from the burning house;
this is the intended meaning of the final testament.
However, when Śākyamuni first appeared in the world,
he first showed three types of people each using the four foundations of mindfulness;
this is like the sheep, deer, and ox carts in the *Lotus Sūtra* that each emerge from the burning house.
Next, it is explained that three types of persons cultivate a single foundation of mindfulness together.
This is as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "This vehicle departs from the triple world and dwells within all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
It is also as described in the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, where those of the three vehicles collectively sever afflictions through the path of ineffable speech.
Next, the sequential cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness by Bodhisattvas is explained.
This is as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Great Perfection of Wisdom),
where the various vehicles of the foundations of mindfulness are distinct and not yet integrated.
Later, it is taught that all the small and great [vehicles] are identical in their single application of mindfulness (*ekasmṛtyupasthāna*).
This is like the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where [all beings] board the same great vehicle and proceed directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Based on this perspective of emptiness, one clarifies all delusions and clarifies all remedies.
This does not contradict any of the sūtras or śāstras.
It is precisely this meaning that is expressed by the statement: "Within a single minute atom, there exists a great thousandfold world-system of sūtra scrolls."
Next, to clarify the inconceivable realm:
within a single thought-moment, the perception of emptiness encompasses the ten dharma-realms;
this is precisely the dharma-nature.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not a remote object;
it is precisely the mind that perceives emptiness.
As the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says:
The liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings;
it should be sought within the sixty-two views.
These three dharmas are not different.
Therefore, turning back upon themselves,
they point out that all sentient beings are themselves bodhi, which cannot be further attained;
this is itself perfect, pure liberation.
The five aggregates are themselves nirvāṇa and cannot be further extinguished;
they are the liberation of purity through skillful means.
The suchness of sentient beings is the suchness of the Buddha.
This is liberation through intrinsic purity.
The liberation of the Buddha consists of the five kinds of nirvana, such as the liberation of form and so forth.
The mind that perceives emptiness is precisely the defiled five aggregates.
The five aggregates are themselves sentient beings,
and sentient beings are themselves the five aggregates;
name-and-form and sentient beings bind one another, unable to be separated.
Contemplating these five aggregates as being nirvana itself, they cannot be further extinguished.
That which is fundamentally without bondage is liberation;
this fundamental liberation encompasses all phenomena.
Therefore, it is said that one seeks liberation within the mind itself.
Furthermore, when one contemplates and perceives that the five aggregates of the mind are themselves the dharma-nature (dharmatā),
one no longer perceives the five aggregates of the mind as separate from it.
By the cessation of this form, one attains the five aggregates of the dharma-nature, such as eternal form;
by the cessation of sentient beings, one attains the eternally abiding sentient beings of the dharma-nature;
and one is able to make one form all forms.
One consciousness contains all consciousnesses;
one sentient being contains all sentient beings,
without mutual obstruction.
Just as a clear mirror manifests all forms and images,
this is called "purity by nature.
These three types of liberation cannot be separated from one another.
Neither vertical nor horizontal, it is inconceivable;
it is sought within the perfect fulfillment of the view of emptiness.
This is called the inconceivable realm.
Within this very realm, the dharmatā of ignorance is perfectly complete;
having grieved over my own former delusion, I have only now awakened to this realization.
All sentient beings are likewise thus.
Since this is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), why not give rise to loving-kindness?
Since this is ignorance (*avidyā*), why not give rise to compassion?
Contemplate this emptiness; see that the fundamental nature is empty, quiescent, and pure like space.
Skillfully settling the mind, one investigates these two dharmas; thus,
the four propositions regarding the view of the aggregates and the view of the provisional do not arise,
whether in their simple or combined forms.
Every phrase contains suffering and its accumulation, obscured by ignorance;
every phrase penetrates the path and its cessation.
Contemplating emptiness, one sees that within a single aggregate (skandha) all aggregates are present.
When the three truths are unmoving, one realizes the Dharmakāya.
Contemplating that the aggregates of non-motion are neither pure nor impure,
even the twin trees of Nirvāṇa are the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
This contemplation is called *prajñā*.
The shattering of the eight inversions is called liberation.
Within a single station of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one gives rise to all stations of mindfulness to tame sentient beings.
These three dharmas are neither cause nor effect.
To regard that which is not the cause as the cause is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);
to regard that which is not the fruit as the fruit is to enter nirvana between the twin trees.
While remaining unmoved within the view of emptiness, one cultivates the inconceivable thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Thus, universally deconstructing [all views] so that the view of emptiness itself cannot be apprehended is called the samādhi of emptiness.
Not perceiving the characteristic of emptiness is called the samādhi of signlessness.
This samādhi, which does not arise from true conditions, is called the "unconditioned" (anabhisaṃskāra) samādhi.
If one does not enter it, one should give rise to a great vow:
internally relinquishing grasping at views and externally casting away life and wealth.
The view of emptiness deviates from principle and the precepts are not pure;
I vow to ensure that this view of emptiness does not violate the Dharma-body,
and to guard the seven branches of discipline so as not to distress sentient beings.
If the view of emptiness cannot be stabilized amidst the clamor and agitation [of worldly distractions],
I now vow that even if suffering reaches my very core, I shall settle my mind in the view of emptiness.
Just as a bridge, the earth, and the ocean remain unmoved even when all things converge upon them, so too shall my body and mind never waver.
If views of emptiness are interspersed,
one must vow to remain purely focused and single-minded, flowing into them moment by moment;
otherwise, if the view of emptiness causes agitation, one will be unable to abide in stillness.
With utmost sincerity, repent and cease the two types of攀緣 (pān-luán-yuán, objective clinging).
If the all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) does not open, it is because ignorance has not been shattered.
Vow to contemplate emptiness so that the *dharmatā* may manifest before you.
With firm resolve and courageous progress, one does not rest until realization is attained.
In this way, these counteractive measures assist in opening the way to nirvana;
by deeply understanding the stages and positions, one avoids conflating them with higher levels.
Neither external nor internal winds and dust can destroy it.

Mind after mind is quiescent and extinguished, flowing into the ocean of sarvajñā.
